species.label: Planarian
species.plain: A freshwater flatworm that regrows its whole body from a fragment; it is the planarian the databases know best, with 1,588 UniProtKB entries, more than all other planarians together, and a chromosome-scale genome with predicted genes.

method: Species: UniProt holds 1,588 entries for Schmidtea mediterranea (4 reviewed), more than half of the 2,784 it holds for all planarians (the order Tricladida; among the others, Dugesia japonica 499, Girardia tigrina 81, Schmidtea polychroa 74, Dugesia ryukyuensis 23), and a proteome for no planarian. WormBase ParaSite holds a chromosome-scale genome assembly of Schmidtea mediterranea with gene models; the assembly is described by Ivanković and others 2024. So the atlas is of Schmidtea mediterranea.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources, and what was read but not copied is in not_copied.

Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates: the InterPro signatures they carry were read from UniProt, and one or two that mark the family were chosen. The build checks that the candidates carry them.
Curated entries first: UniProt has 4 reviewed entries for the species, and none belongs to a family the atlas draws.
Named in a publication: a planarian protein counts as named only where the saved abstract, or the saved open-access text, of the paper uses the name. 4 products rest on this.

Family signature: unreviewed UniProtKB entries of the species that carry the signature, and gene models that carry it. The gene models are those of one genome annotation (WBPS19 of WormBase ParaSite, assembly schMedS3_haplotype1): 17,294 genes with a predicted protein. The ones the atlas names are listed in data/proteins/planarian/reference_proteins.tsv. A model carries a signature if that annotation's own InterPro matches say so, or if its predicted protein is, letter for letter, a sequence that carries it in UniProt's archive (InterPro 111.0).
A UniProtKB sequence and a gene model are given as one product when at least 80% of the sequence's 8-residue words occur in the model's predicted protein and no other gene reaches half of that share.

Where a signature found nothing, it was also asked of all 98,660 planarian sequences in UniProt's archive, of the UniProtKB entries of all flatworms and of reviewed human entries; the unit's note gives what came back.

Each product says, apart, how it was found (named in a publication, by the signature of a family that makes the machine, or only by that of a family that goes with it, such as a beta subunit or a regulator) and what its record is (a UniProtKB entry, reviewed or not, or a gene model of the genome annotation).

A product found by the signature of a family that makes the machine is a candidate, never an established counterpart; one found only by that of a family that goes with the machine is no candidate for the machine's own work. Counts are gene models in one haplotype of one genome assembly, not genes confirmed in the animal, and short models may be fragments.
No similarity search against other species was run, and no product is called an ortholog.

sources.licence: No restriction on use is stated: the database's disclaimer says "Ensembl imposes no restrictions on access to, or use of, the data provided". It asks that a genome's paper and the database be cited, asks users of an unpublished genome to tell its owners before a large-scale analysis, and warns that third-party constraints may apply. The paper taken to describe this genome is CC BY 4.0.
sources.cite: Howe and others (2017) WormBase ParaSite - a comprehensive resource for helminth genomics. Mol Biochem Parasitol 215:2-10. Genome: Ivanković and others (2024) A comparative analysis of planarian genomes reveals regulatory conservation in the face of rapid structural divergence. Nat Commun 15:8215. The database's page of this annotation names no paper. That it is the annotation this paper describes is inferred, not stated by either: the assembly has the paper's name (schMedS3 haplotype 1), the count of coding genes in the second haplotype is the same in both (21,310), and in the first it is 21,392 here against the paper's 21,401.

not_copied: The catalogue of planarian proteins detected by mass spectrometry (Ying and others 2025, doi:10.1016/j.devcel.2025.08.015) was not copied: the paper and its supplementary tables reserve all rights, and its public deposit (ProteomeXchange PXD042308, which iProX's data licence puts under CC0) holds instrument files and sample sheets, not the list of proteins. PlanMine was read and nothing taken from it, because its front page states no licence or terms of use, only how to cite it. Abstracts and article texts were read to check names and are not copied. Of the papers that name the proteins listed here, Oviedo and Levin 2007, Wagner and others 2012, Wenemoser and others 2012, Abascal and Zardoya 2013, Beane and others 2013 and Arenas and others 2017 state no open licence: each is cited for a name, which a sequence record or a UniProtKB entry carries too, and none of their findings is repeated.

U01.note: 3 planarian gene models carry the signature of the sodium channel's pore subunit, and a 2014 paper named 3 short planarian sequences as sodium channels (scna-1 to scna-3), which match 2 of those gene models. None can be singled out as the counterpart of NaV1.2. No planarian sequence carries the signature of the beta subunits (IPR027098); it marks 2 reviewed human entries.

U38.note: There is no connexin 40 or connexin 37 to find in a planarian: by its signatures it has innexins, another family of gap-junction proteins, and no connexins. 68 planarian gene models carry the innexin signature and none the connexin one; no UniProtKB entry of any flatworm carries the connexin signature either, while 21 reviewed human entries do. One planarian innexin has a sequence record of its own, smedinx-11. More is to be read in Abascal and Zardoya 2013, on which animals have each family, and in Oviedo and Levin 2007, on that innexin; neither states an open licence, so nothing is taken from them. Nothing says which innexins, if any, would form a channel like this one.
